relationship: later use of the coming-one promise to encourage endurance
rationale: Habakkuk commands waiting if he delays because the coming one will come and not linger. Hebrews likewise urges endurance before repeating that the coming One will come and not delay. Both place the promise within an exhortation to patient expectation.
source_text: For the vision is still for a season, and it will rise toward the end and not toward emptiness. If he delays, wait for him, for coming he will come and certainly will not linger.

target_units.text: For you need endurance, so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the promise.
“For yet a very little while, the coming One will come and will not delay.

relationship: later quotation joining righteous life and the danger of drawing back
rationale: Habakkuk says God's soul takes no pleasure in one drawing back and that the righteous one lives by My faithfulness. Hebrews repeats both clauses in reversed order, saying My righteous one lives by faith. The connection preserves the distinct placement of My and the native faithfulness wording.
source_text: If he draws back, My soul has no pleasure in him; but the righteous one shall live by My faithfulness.

target_units.text: But My righteous one will live by faith; and if he draws back, My soul takes no pleasure in him.”
But we are not people who draw back to destruction, but people of faith for the preservation of the soul.

relationship: explicit later use of the righteous-one life statement
rationale: Habakkuk declares that the righteous one lives by My faithfulness. Romans introduces Scripture saying the righteous one lives by faith within its account of the gospel and God's righteousness. The shared statement is direct, while Habakkuk's possessive and faithfulness wording remain distinct.
source_text: If he draws back, My soul has no pleasure in him; but the righteous one shall live by My faithfulness.

target_units.text: For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is God’s power for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.
For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written, “But the righteous one will live by faith.”

relationship: later use of the righteous-one statement in discussion of law and faith
rationale: Habakkuk says the righteous one lives by My faithfulness. Galatians quotes the righteous one living by faith while arguing about justification before God and law. The later argumentative use is recorded without silently replacing the source's My faithfulness wording.
source_text: If he draws back, My soul has no pleasure in him; but the righteous one shall live by My faithfulness.

target_units.text: For all who are of works of law are under a curse, for it is written, “Accursed is everyone who does not abide by all the things written in the book of the law, to do them.”
Now it is clear that no one is justified before God by law, because “The righteous one will live by faith.”
But the law is not of faith; rather, “The one who does these things will live by them.”

relationship: insatiable human appetite compared to Hades
rationale: Habakkuk portrays the boastful conqueror's appetite as Hades and death, never filled despite gathered peoples. Proverbs likewise says Hades and destruction are not filled and compares them with insatiable human eyes. Both expressly link human insatiability with Hades.
source_text: But the wine-soaked, contemptuous, boastful man will accomplish nothing. He widened his appetite like Hades and is like death, never filled; he will gather all nations and receive all peoples to himself.

target_units.text: Hades and destruction are not filled, and likewise human eyes are insatiable.

relationship: a saying taken up against an oppressive ruler
rationale: Habakkuk announces a parable and riddle taken up against one accumulating what is not his. Isaiah likewise introduces a lament against Babylon's king after release from harsh slavery and describes the taskmaster's end. Both turn the oppressor into the subject of a public saying after exploitation.
source_text: Will not all these take up a parable against him and a riddle for his account? They will say, ‘Woe to the one multiplying for himself what is not his—how long?—and heavily weighting his collar!’

target_units.text: On that day God will give you rest from pain, your wrath and the harsh slavery in which you served them,
and you will take up this lament against Babylon’s king and say on that day, “How the one who made demands has rested, and the taskmaster rested!
God shattered the sinners’ yoke, the rulers’ yoke;
having struck a nation in wrath with an incurable blow, striking a nation with a blow of anger that did not spare,
he rested confidently. The whole earth cries out with gladness,

relationship: same-chapter plunder threatened and explained as reversal
rationale: Habakkuk 2:7 tells the addressed oppressor that he will become plunder when adversaries rise. The following verse explains that remaining peoples will despoil him because he despoiled many nations. The next unit gives the explicit reciprocal reason for the threatened loss.
source_text: For suddenly those biting him will rise, and those plotting against you will awake; you will become their plunder.

target_units.text: Because you despoiled many nations, all the remaining peoples will despoil you, because of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all its inhabitants.

relationship: recompense corresponding to harm done to others
rationale: Habakkuk says the despoiler of many nations will himself be despoiled by remaining peoples. Obadiah likewise announces that what was done will return upon the doer's own head. Both explicitly state reciprocal judgment, with Habakkuk specifying plunder and bloodshed.
source_text: Because you despoiled many nations, all the remaining peoples will despoil you, because of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all its inhabitants.

target_units.text: For the day of the Lord is near against all the nations. Just as you acted, so it will be for you; your recompense will be repaid upon your own head.

relationship: a high nest imagined as security from danger
rationale: Habakkuk condemns setting a nest high to escape evils while acquiring evil gain. Obadiah likewise describes a high dwelling, imagined security from being brought down and a nest among stars from which God will bring its occupant down. Both challenge safety sought through elevated habitation.
source_text: O you who acquire evil gain for your house, setting your nest on high to escape the hand of evils!

target_units.text: The pride of your heart has lifted you up, you who camp in holes in the rocks, raising his dwelling high and saying in his heart, “Who will bring me down to the ground?”
If you soar like an eagle, and if you place your nest among the stars, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord.

relationship: a house established through wrongdoing becomes an accusation
rationale: Habakkuk says the plot brought shame upon the house and involved the end of many peoples. Jeremiah likewise condemns a house built without righteousness, unpaid labor, greed and innocent blood. Both connect the household's apparent advancement with culpable harm.
source_text: You planned shame for your house, brought many peoples to an end, and your soul sinned.

target_units.text: O you who build your house without righteousness and your upper rooms without judgment! He works through his neighbor without payment and will not give him his wages.
You built yourself a well-proportioned house, airy upper rooms set apart by windows, paneled with cedar and painted with red ocher.
Will you reign because you are provoked in Ahaz your father? They will not eat or drink. It was better for you to do judgment and good righteousness.
They did not know; they did not judge a case for the lowly or a case for the poor. Is this not your failing to know Me? says the Lord.
Behold, neither your eyes nor your heart are good; instead they are directed toward your greed, innocent blood to shed it, wrongdoing, and murder to commit it.

relationship: stones given the role of crying out
rationale: Habakkuk depicts a stone crying from a wall and a beetle from wood uttering words. Jesus likewise says that stones will cry out if the disciples fall silent. The personified stone's speech is shared; the settings differ, and no beam is substituted for Habakkuk's beetle.
source_text: For a stone will cry from a wall, and a beetle from wood will utter these things.

target_units.text: And some of the Pharisees from the crowd said to Him, “Teacher, rebuke Thy disciples.”
And He answered, “I tell you, if these fall silent, the stones will cry out.”

relationship: building a city with bloodshed and injustice
rationale: Habakkuk condemns building a city with bloodshed and preparing it with injustices. Micah likewise addresses leaders who build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with injustices. The distinctive paired accusation directly connects the passages.
source_text: Woe to the one building a city with bloodshed and preparing a city with injustices!

target_units.text: Hear these things now, leaders of Jacob’s house and remaining ones of Israel’s house, who abhor justice and twist all straight things,
you who build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with injustices!

relationship: earth filled with knowledge of the Lord compared to covering waters
rationale: Habakkuk announces the earth filled with knowing the Lord's glory as water covers. Isaiah likewise declares the whole earth filled with knowledge of the Lord as abundant water covers the seas. Both combine universal knowledge of God with the covering-water comparison.
source_text: For the earth will be filled with knowing the Lord’s glory, as water will cover them.

target_units.text: And they will certainly do no harm, nor will they be able at all to destroy anyone upon My holy mountain; for the whole earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant water covers the seas.

relationship: the cup of divine judgment passes to those who harmed others
rationale: Habakkuk commands the aggressor to drink dishonor because the cup from the Lord's right hand has reached him. Isaiah describes the Lord's cup of anger taken from Jerusalem and thrown into its oppressors' hands. Both portray judgment through a cup reaching wrongdoers.
source_text: Drink, you too, a fullness of dishonor instead of glory; be tossed and shaken! The cup of the Lord’s right hand has come around to you, and dishonor has gathered upon your glory.

target_units.text: Awake, awake, rise, Jerusalem, you who drank the cup of anger from the Lord’s hand. You drank out and emptied the cup of falling, the bowl of anger.
There was no one to comfort you among all your children you bore, and no one to take your hand among all your sons you raised.
These two confront you—who will grieve with you?—fall and crushing, famine and sword. Who will comfort you?
Your sons are helpless, sleeping at every way out like a half-boiled beet, full of the Lord’s anger, exhausted because of the Lord God.
Therefore listen, humbled one, drunk but not from wine.
Thus says the Lord God who judges His people: ‘Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of falling, the bowl of anger. You will not drink it again.
I will throw it into the hands of those who wronged and humbled you, who told your soul, “Bend down, so we may pass.” You laid your back level with the earth, outside for passersby.’”

relationship: same-chapter repeated indictment for bloodshed and impiety
rationale: Both units expressly accuse the addressed power of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all inhabitants. The repeated charge connects the woes while 2:17 also names Lebanon and wild animals, details absent from 2:8.
source_text: For Lebanon’s impiety will cover you, and the misery of wild animals will terrify you, because of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all its inhabitants.

target_units.text: Because you despoiled many nations, all the remaining peoples will despoil you, because of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all its inhabitants.

relationship: the futility of worshiping objects made by their worshipers
rationale: Habakkuk questions the use of carved and cast objects and the maker's trust in mute idols. Isaiah likewise calls fashioned gods useless and narrates a craftsman making an image from wood and worshiping it. Both expose reliance on human fabrication.
source_text: What use is a carved image, that they carved it? They formed it as a cast object, a false appearance, because its maker trusted his creation, making mute idols.

target_units.text: All who fashion and carve are futile, making what pleases them, things that will not help them. But they will be ashamed—
all who fashion a god and carve useless things,
and all from whom they came have dried up. Let the deaf from among humankind all assemble and stand together; let them be abashed and ashamed together.
For a craftsman sharpened iron, worked it with an adze, bored it with a drill, and worked it with his strong arm. He will hunger and grow weak and certainly not drink water. Having selected
wood, a craftsman set it by measure and arranged it with glue. He made it like a man’s form and human beauty, to set it in a house.
The wood he cut from the woodland was what the Lord planted and rain made grow,
so that it might serve people for burning. Taking some, he warmed himself; after burning it they baked loaves over the pieces. They worked the rest into gods and worship them.

Half of it they burned in fire, and after burning it they baked loaves over the pieces. Over it he roasted meat, ate, and was satisfied. Warmed, he said, ‘It is pleasant for me, for I am warm and have seen fire!’
He made the rest into a carved god and worships it and prays, saying, ‘Rescue me, for you are my god.’

relationship: wood adorned with precious metal cannot act as a living being
rationale: Habakkuk mocks calling wood to wake and stone to rise, describing a gold-and-silver plate with no breath. Jeremiah likewise describes worked wood adorned with gold and silver, unable to move or take a step. Both oppose the decorated object to the powers expected of life.
source_text: Woe to the one saying to wood, ‘Wake and rise!’ and to stone, ‘Be lifted up!’ It is an appearance, a plate of gold and silver, and no breath at all is in it.

target_units.text: For the nations’ customs are futile: it is wood cut from the woodland, a carpenter’s work and a cast object.
They are adorned with silver and gold; with hammers and nails they fastened them, and they will not move.
They must be lifted and carried, because they will not take a step. Do not fear them, because they certainly will not do evil, and no good is in them.

relationship: cast images have no living spirit
rationale: Habakkuk explicitly says the decorated image has no breath at all. Jeremiah likewise says cast objects are false and have no spirit in them, then calls them futile works that perish. Both deny life to the fabricated object.
source_text: Woe to the one saying to wood, ‘Wake and rise!’ and to stone, ‘Be lifted up!’ It is an appearance, a plate of gold and silver, and no breath at all is in it.

target_units.text: Every human became foolish, without knowledge; every goldsmith was put to shame at his carved things, because they cast false things; there is no spirit in them.
They are futile, mocked works; at the time of their visitation they will perish.
